q: What operation did she have?
s: Mrs. Kawthar, 72, had an operation six weeks ago after years of hip pain. Today she bent low to pick up her slipper while sitting on a soft sofa and felt a clunk. Her leg is now short and turned in. An X-ray shows the metal ball has come out of its plastic cup. She was told after surgery not to bend her hip past a right angle.
c: A metal ball out of its plastic cup after bending low, weeks after an operation for hip pain.

a.w: In the first weeks it can dislocate if the hip bends too far, which is why patients avoid low seats and bending deep.
A keyhole operation that leaves no metal ball.
Screws hold a broken neck of the femur; there is no ball and cup.
The wrong joint.

lq: What movement is avoided early after a hip replacement?
la: Bending the hip past a right angle (low seats, deep bending)

q: Why did her inhaler not work?
s: Sondos, 6, has asthma and wakes coughing at night. She has a preventer inhaler twice a day, but nothing improves. At the clinic she shows how she uses it: she presses it straight into her mouth while breathing out, and most of the mist hits her cheek. She has never used the plastic tube that came with it.
c: A child pressing the inhaler while breathing out, mist on her cheek, and an unused plastic tube.

a.w: Young children can't time the puff with a breath. A spacer holds the mist so it reaches the lungs.
She doesn't take it, and her problem is technique, not the drug.
Not needed if the preventer reaches her lungs.
Asthma isn't an infection.

lq: What helps children get inhaler medicine into the lungs?

q: Which tablet did she stop suddenly?
s: Mrs. Rehab, 41, took a daily tablet for anxiety and depression for two years. She felt better and stopped it all at once. Three days later she feels dizzy, has "electric shock" feelings in her head when she moves her eyes, feels sick, irritable and has vivid dreams. She has no fever and her bloods are normal.
c: Brain-zaps, dizziness and vivid dreams days after a daily anxiety tablet was stopped at once.

a.w: SSRIs with a short life, especially paroxetine, cause withdrawal when stopped suddenly. They are stopped slowly.
It lasts long in the body, so stopping it rarely causes withdrawal.
Stopping it risks a relapse of mania, not brain-zaps.
Stopping it suddenly can cause fits and shakes, not mainly brain-zaps.

lq: Which SSRI causes the worst withdrawal when stopped suddenly?

q: Which tablet damaged his lungs?
s: Mr. Sabry, 70, has had an irregular heartbeat for two years, controlled on a daily tablet. His skin turns blue-grey in the sun, and last year his thyroid became underactive. Now he is short of breath on walking, with a dry cough. His CT shows scarring in both lungs. He never smoked and never worked with dust.
c: A heart rhythm tablet, blue-grey skin, thyroid trouble, and lung scarring.

a.w: Long use can scar the lungs, upset the thyroid and turn the skin blue-grey.
It can worsen asthma but doesn't scar the lungs.
It doesn't scar the lungs or upset the thyroid.
It doesn't affect the lungs this way.

lq: Which heart rhythm drug can scar the lungs and upset the thyroid?

q: Which tablet should not have been given with her methotrexate?
s: Mrs. Fawzia, 63, has rheumatoid arthritis on weekly methotrexate. She went to a walk-in clinic with a urine infection and was given an antibiotic twice a day for a week. Now she has mouth ulcers, a fever and bruises, and her blood count is very low. She took the methotrexate correctly, once a week.
c: Weekly methotrexate, a new antibiotic for a urine infection, then a crashed blood count.

a.w: It also blocks folate, so with methotrexate it can wipe out the bone marrow. The two are not given together.
A safer choice for a urine infection with methotrexate.
It doesn't block folate like trimethoprim.
It is safe with methotrexate.

lq: Which antibiotic is dangerous with methotrexate?

q: What was missed that let her lungs fill?
s: Mrs. Nawal, 70, had bowel surgery two days ago. Her belly is swollen and silent, and she is vomiting green fluid again and again. Overnight, while lying flat, she breathed some vomit into her lungs and now has a fever and crackles on the right. The nurses had kept her eating soup and had not put any tube in.
c: A swollen, silent belly after surgery with green vomiting, food continued, and no tube.

a.o: Nasogastric tube with nil by mouth
a.w: In a stopped bowel, a tube through the nose drains the stomach and stops vomiting that can go into the lungs.
They don't help a stopped bowel and can make vomiting worse.
It doesn't empty the stomach.
It helps the bowel restart, but doesn't stop vomiting now.

lq: What is the first step in a stopped bowel after surgery with vomiting?
la: Nil by mouth and a nasogastric tube to drain the stomach

q: What should be done while waiting for the ambulance?
s: A man in his 40s collapses at a bus stop. He doesn't answer when spoken to or gently shaken, but he is breathing normally, his chest rising and falling. There is no sign of a neck injury and he didn't fall from a height. A passer-by has called an ambulance and is still on the phone.
c: Unresponsive but breathing normally, with no sign of a neck injury.

a.w: Rolling him onto his side keeps the airway open and lets any vomit drain. Keep checking his breathing.
CPR is only for someone not breathing normally.
Never give anything by mouth to an unresponsive person.

a.o: Sit him up against the wall
a.w: He may slump and block his airway.

lq: What is done for someone unresponsive but breathing normally?
la: Place them in the recovery position and keep checking breathing

q: Which daily tablet lowered his cholesterol?
s: Mr. Wahid, 56, had a heart attack last year and had a stent put in. Since then he takes a small tablet every night. His LDL cholesterol has fallen from 4.6 to 1.6. He has had no new chest pain. Last month he had sore thigh muscles for a while, and his CK test was checked and came back normal.
c: A nightly tablet after a heart attack, a big fall in LDL, and sore muscles with a CK check.

a.w: Statins lower LDL cholesterol and cut the risk of another heart attack. Muscle aches are a known side effect, so CK is checked.
It stops platelets clumping but doesn't lower cholesterol.
It slows the heart and doesn't lower cholesterol.
A platelet drug used after stents, not a cholesterol drug.

lq: Which drugs lower LDL cholesterol after a heart attack?

q: Which new tablet caused the skin to peel?
s: Mr. Kamal, 52, was started on a tablet three weeks ago to stop his gout coming back. Now he has a fever, sore red eyes, painful mouth ulcers, and his skin is blistering and peeling in sheets over his chest and back. Gentle rubbing makes the skin slide off. He takes no other new medicines.
c: A new gout-prevention tablet weeks ago, then fever, mouth ulcers and skin peeling in sheets.

a.w: It is one of the commonest causes of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, usually in the first weeks.
It treats attacks and causes diarrhea, not peeling skin.
It very rarely causes this, and it isn't a gout preventer.
It treats gout pain, and isn't the new preventer here.

lq: Which gout drug is a common cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

q: What should be done next?
s: Mr. Medhat, 68, has had a nosebleed from his right nostril for 40 minutes. He sat leaning forward and pinched the soft part of his nose firmly for 20 minutes, twice, but it is still bleeding. His pressure is 150/90 and his pulse is steady. He takes no blood thinners. The doctor can't see a bleeding point at the front.
c: A nosebleed that didn't stop after 20 minutes of firm pinching, twice, with no point seen at the front.

a.w: When pinching fails and no point can be cauterized, a pack or balloon in the nose presses on the bleeding.
It makes blood run down the throat and doesn't stop the bleeding.
It doesn't stop a bleed that pinching couldn't.
They may help a little, but they don't stop an active bleed now.

lq: What is done when a nosebleed doesn't stop with pinching?
la: Cautery if a point is seen, otherwise nasal packing

q: What antidote is given?
s: Mr. Sayed, 50, a mechanic, drank from a bottle in his garage, thinking it was a sweet drink. Hours later he seems drunk but there is no alcohol on his breath. His blood is very acidic, with a large gap between measured and calculated salts. His kidneys are starting to fail, and his urine has crystals in it.
c: A sweet drink from a garage, drunk without alcohol, very acidic blood, and crystals in the urine.

a.w: It blocks the enzyme that turns ethylene glycol (antifreeze) into its toxic acids. Ethanol works the same way if fomepizole isn't available.
It reverses opioids, which don't cause acidic blood and crystals.
The antidote for paracetamol, not antifreeze.
For insecticide poisoning, not antifreeze.

lq: What is the antidote for ethylene glycol poisoning?

q: Which drip closed her ketone gap?
s: Shahd, 17, has type 1 diabetes and has vomited for a day. She is breathing deep and fast, her breath smells of pear drops, and she is dehydrated. Her sugar is 28, her blood ketones are very high and her blood is acidic. She is given fluids and a second drip at a fixed rate by weight. Over 12 hours, her ketones clear.
c: Type 1 diabetes, high ketones, acidic blood, and a second drip at a fixed rate by weight.

a.w: A fixed-rate insulin drip stops the body making ketones, while fluids replace what was lost.
It raises sugar, the opposite of what she needs.
Rarely used; it doesn't stop ketones being made.
A tablet for type 2 diabetes. It doesn't treat ketoacidosis.

lq: What treats diabetic ketoacidosis?
la: IV fluids and a fixed-rate insulin infusion (with potassium)

q: Which tablet should not have been given?
s: Ziad, 25, came back from a trip with fever, belly cramps and bloody diarrhea. A pharmacist gave him a tablet to stop the diarrhea, and he took several. Now the diarrhea has stopped, but his belly is swollen, very tender and silent, and an X-ray shows a hugely widened large bowel. He is getting sicker.
c: Fever with bloody diarrhea, a tablet that stopped the stools, then a hugely swollen bowel.

a.w: In bloody diarrhea with fever it can trap germs and toxins and cause a dangerously swollen bowel, so it is avoided.
The right treatment for diarrhea, and they don't swell the bowel.
It eases fever and doesn't stop the bowel.
Sometimes used for traveler's diarrhea, and it doesn't swell the bowel.

lq: When should loperamide be avoided?
la: In bloody diarrhea or diarrhea with fever

q: Which malaria drug caused this?
s: Mr. Badr, 24, from a family with a known blood enzyme problem, was treated for malaria after a work trip. Two days into a second tablet meant to stop the malaria coming back, his urine turns dark like cola, he is pale and yellow, and he is tired. His blood shows broken red cells with "bite" marks.
c: A family blood enzyme problem, a second malaria tablet, then dark urine and broken red cells with bite marks.

a.w: In G6PD deficiency it breaks the red cells. G6PD is checked before it is given.
It treats the malaria attack and doesn't break red cells in G6PD.
Usually safe in G6PD deficiency at normal doses.
It is used to prevent malaria and doesn't break red cells.

lq: Which malaria drug must be checked against G6PD first?

q: What does she need next for her bleeding?
s: Mrs. Hayam, 66, is having chemotherapy for leukemia. Today she has bleeding gums, small red dots all over her legs and a nosebleed that won't stop. Her hemoglobin is 9.5 and her white cells are low, but her platelet count is 6. Her clotting tests are normal. She has no fever.
c: Bleeding with a platelet count of 6 during chemotherapy, normal clotting tests.

a.w: With platelets this low and bleeding, she needs platelets straight away.
Her hemoglobin is acceptable; red cells won't stop the bleeding.
It replaces clotting factors, and her clotting tests are normal.
It helps clotting factors, not platelets.

lq: What is given for bleeding with very low platelets?

q: What would have prevented this?
s: Mr. Tarek, 33, went on a two-week work trip to a malaria area in Africa. He took no tablets before going and used no mosquito net. His colleague took a daily tablet from before the trip until weeks after coming home and stayed well. Ten days after Tarek returned he has fever and shaking chills, and a blood film shows malaria.
c: A trip to a malaria area, a colleague who took a daily tablet and stayed well.

a.w: Tablets such as atovaquone-proguanil or doxycycline, with nets and repellents, prevent malaria in travelers.
It protects against typhoid, not malaria.
It protects against yellow fever, not malaria.
It protects against hepatitis A only.

lq: What prevents malaria in travelers?
la: Prevention tablets plus nets and repellents

q: Which added tablet pushed her potassium up?
s: Mrs. Nagwa, 72, has a weak heart and takes ramipril. Last month her heart doctor added another tablet that also helps the heart. Today her potassium is 6.6, and her ECG shows peaked T waves. Her kidney numbers are a little worse. She also eats lots of bananas and oranges, as she always has.
c: Ramipril plus a newly added heart tablet, and a potassium of 6.6.

a.w: It keeps potassium in the body. With an ACE inhibitor like ramipril, potassium can climb dangerously.
It lowers potassium, the opposite.
It doesn't raise potassium much.
Low potassium makes it toxic, but it doesn't raise potassium.

lq: Which two heart drugs together raise potassium?

q: What should he be given now?
s: Mr. Hamdi, 64, suddenly couldn't move his right arm or speak properly while watching TV, 90 minutes ago. His wife called an ambulance at once. His brain scan shows no bleeding. His pressure is 170/95, his sugar is normal, and he takes no blood thinners. He had no surgery or bleeding recently.
c: A sudden stroke 90 minutes ago, no bleeding on the scan, and no reason to avoid clot-busting.

a.w: A clot-busting drug given within 4.5 hours of a clot stroke can restore blood flow. A scan must first rule out bleeding.
It is given later or if clot-busting isn't possible, but it doesn't dissolve the clot now.

a.o: Lower his pressure to normal fast
a.w: A big drop can harm the brain; it is only lowered if very high before clot-busting.

a.o: Wait to see if it passes
a.w: Every minute of waiting loses brain cells.

lq: What is the time window for clot-busting in stroke?
la: Within 4.5 hours of onset, after a scan rules out bleeding

q: What stopped the bleeding?
s: Rania, 31, has just given birth to her fourth baby after a long labor. Ten minutes later she is bleeding heavily, and her womb feels soft and floppy when pressed through her belly. The midwife rubs the womb firmly and gives an injection. The womb hardens under her hand and the bleeding slows.
c: Heavy bleeding just after birth, a soft womb, then an injection that made it hard.

a.w: It makes the womb contract, which squeezes the bleeding vessels shut. A soft womb is the commonest cause of bleeding after birth.
It prevents eclamptic fits and actually relaxes the womb.
It prevents Rh disease, not bleeding.
It relaxes the womb and is used to slow early labor, the opposite.

lq: What is the first drug for bleeding after birth from a soft womb?

q: Which tablet triggered her eye attack?
s: Mrs. Hoda, 60, is long-sighted. Last night she took a tablet for a cold that "dries the nose". In the dim cinema her right eye became red and very painful, with blurred vision and halos around lights, and she vomited. Her eye feels hard as stone and her pupil is mid-sized and doesn't react to light.
c: A long-sighted woman, a drying cold tablet, a dark room, then a hard, painful red eye with halos.

a.w: Drugs that widen the pupil, such as drying antihistamines, can close the narrow drainage angle in a long-sighted eye and cause acute glaucoma.
It doesn't widen the pupil.
It doesn't affect the eye.
It doesn't act on the pupil.

lq: What kind of drug can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma?
la: Drugs that widen the pupil, such as antihistamines and anticholinergics

q: What should be done for the shoulder?
s: Hamza, 22, fell on his outstretched arm during a football match. His right shoulder looks squared off, he holds his arm slightly out from his body, and he can't move it. Feeling on the outer arm, over the badge area, is normal, and his pulse is strong. An X-ray shows the ball of the shoulder lying in front of its socket, with no fracture.
c: A squared-off shoulder with the ball in front of the socket, no fracture, and normal nerve and pulse.

a.w: Putting the ball back in its socket, then checking nerves and taking a new X-ray, is the treatment.
Usually not needed for a first, simple dislocation.
Without putting it back, the shoulder stays dislocated.
The joint must be put back first.

lq: What is the first treatment for an anterior shoulder dislocation?
la: Closed reduction, then a sling and a repeat X-ray

q: What fixed her dehydration?
s: Lama, 2, has had watery diarrhea and some vomiting for two days. She is a little sleepy, her mouth is dry, and she cries without tears, but she drinks when offered. The nurse gave her mother a drink to give in small sips every few minutes with a spoon. Four hours later Lama is passing urine and playing again.
c: A mildly dehydrated toddler who can drink, given small sips every few minutes.

a.w: Small, frequent sips of salts and sugar in water replace what diarrhea takes out. Most children don't need a drip.
Too much sugar and too little salt; it can make diarrhea worse.
Not given to young children with diarrhea.
Kept for children who are badly dehydrated or can't drink.

lq: What is the first treatment for mild dehydration from diarrhea in children?
la: Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips

q: Which drug caused this?
s: Mr. Akram, 28, was admitted with a first episode of psychosis and was started on injections of a strong drug for it. Four days later he is very stiff all over, like lead pipes, with a temperature of 40, sweating, a racing heart and swinging pressure. He is confused, and his CK is very high. His reflexes are normal and his pupils are normal.
c: A new strong antipsychotic, then lead-pipe stiffness, high fever and a very high CK, with normal reflexes.

a.w: Strong dopamine blockers can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, fever and a high CK, over days.
It can cause serotonin syndrome, with jerks and brisk reflexes, not lead-pipe stiffness.
It is used to treat this syndrome, not cause it.
Toxicity causes tremor and confusion, not this pattern.

lq: What causes neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

q: What brought his lung back up?
s: Mr. Nader, 25, tall and thin, felt a sudden sharp pain in his right chest and became breathless. The X-ray shows a big rim of air around a collapsed right lung. His oxygen is 92%. A thin tube is put between his ribs and connected to a water bottle that bubbles. The next X-ray shows the lung back up against the chest wall.
c: A big collapsed lung from trapped air, a tube between the ribs, and a bubbling water bottle.

a.w: A tube lets the trapped air out through a water seal, so the lung can re-expand.
It helps small ones heal slowly, but this is a big one with breathlessness.
There is no infection.
Far too much; a simple drain works.

lq: How is a large pneumothorax with breathlessness treated?
la: Needle aspiration or a chest drain

q: What tablet worked so fast?
s: Mrs. Nabila, 72, has had painful, stiff shoulders and hips for weeks, worst in the mornings, so she can't comb her hair or get out of bed easily. Her ESR is high. She has no headache and no jaw pain. Within two days of starting a low-dose tablet, she is almost back to normal. Her doctor says she'll lower it slowly over months.
c: Older age, stiff shoulders and hips, a high ESR, and dramatic relief within days of a low-dose tablet.

a.w: Polymyalgia rheumatica responds dramatically to low-dose steroids, which are lowered slowly.
Sometimes added later to cut steroid use, but it doesn't work in two days.
It eases pain a little but doesn't work dramatically like this.
It is for gout, not polymyalgia.

lq: What is the treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica?

q: What operation years ago caused this blockage?
s: Mrs. Samira, 50, had her appendix taken out through an open cut at 15, and a cesarean at 30. Now she has cramping belly pain, a swollen belly and green vomiting, and hasn't passed wind for a day. She has no hernia. A scan shows blocked small bowel, with a sudden narrowing and no tumor.
c: Open belly operations years ago, then a small bowel blockage with no hernia and no tumor.

a.w: Scar bands form after belly operations and are the commonest cause of small bowel blockage, even decades later.
She has no hernia, and she never had one repaired.
She never had one.
It doesn't affect the bowel.

lq: What is the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction?

q: What should be done first?
s: At a gym, a man in his 50s suddenly collapses off a treadmill. He doesn't respond to shouting or shaking. He isn't breathing normally, only giving an odd gasp every few seconds. A staff member has called an ambulance on speaker and another is running to fetch the defibrillator on the wall.
c: Unresponsive, only gasping, and a defibrillator on the way.

a.w: Gasping isn't normal breathing. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest until the defibrillator arrives, then use it.
Only for people breathing normally.

a.o: Check his pulse for a full minute
a.w: Wastes time; untrained rescuers don't check pulses.
Compressions matter most; breaths alone don't move blood.

lq: Is gasping normal breathing in a collapsed person?
la: No: start CPR and use a defibrillator

q: Which blood pressure tablet is she switched to?
s: Mrs. Yomna, 33, has had high blood pressure for years, controlled on ramipril. She is now seven weeks pregnant. Her doctor stops the ramipril at once, because it can harm the baby's kidneys, and starts another tablet that is safe in pregnancy. Her pressure stays around 130/85. She has no asthma, and she feels well.
c: A pregnant woman taken off ramipril and moved to a blood pressure tablet that is safe in pregnancy, with no asthma.

a.w: It is the usual first tablet for high blood pressure in pregnancy. It is avoided in asthma, which she doesn't have.
Like ramipril, it harms the baby's kidneys and is avoided in pregnancy.
It can affect the baby's development and isn't used in pregnancy.
Water tablets are not first choice in pregnancy.

lq: Which blood pressure tablet is first choice in pregnancy?

q: What was done to the wart?
s: Mohab, 14, had a rough wart on his finger for a year that didn't go with salicylic acid paint. At the clinic, the doctor sprayed something very cold on it from a can for a few seconds, twice. It stung and turned white. Next day a blister formed under the wart. Two weeks later the blister dried, and the wart came off with it.
c: A very cold spray from a can, a white sting, then a blister that lifted the wart off.

a.w: Freezing kills the infected skin; a blister forms and the wart falls off with it.
It burns the wart with light, not a cold spray.
It needs a scalpel and stitches, and leaves a scar.
A cream used at home, not a cold spray.

lq: How does cryotherapy remove a wart?
la: Freezing with liquid nitrogen makes a blister that lifts the wart off

q: What was done to help him breathe?
s: Mr. Abbas, 63, has a large throat cancer that is narrowing his airway. He is short of breath even at rest, with a harsh noise on breathing in. In theater, a tube was placed through a small cut in the front of his neck, straight into his windpipe, below the cancer. Now he breathes easily, but he has to cover the tube with a finger to speak.
c: A tube through the front of the neck into the windpipe, below a blocking cancer, and speaking by covering it.

a.w: An opening into the windpipe below the blockage lets air in directly.
It removes the tonsils and doesn't bypass a blocked airway.
It stops nosebleeds.
They drain the ear.

lq: What bypasses a blocked upper airway through the neck?

q: Which tablets did she take?
s: Mrs. Ola, 45, has long-term pain and low mood and takes a tablet each night. Her husband found her drowsy next to empty strips. She has a dry mouth, big pupils and hot, dry skin, her heart rate is 130, and she had a fit in the ambulance. Her ECG shows a wide QRS. She is given a sodium bicarbonate drip for her heart.
c: A nightly tablet for pain and mood, big pupils, a dry mouth, a fit, and a wide QRS treated with bicarbonate.

a.w: Tricyclic overdose causes drying effects, fits and a wide QRS. Bicarbonate protects the heart.
Overdose is much safer and rarely widens the QRS.
It looks harmless at first and harms the liver, not the heart rhythm.
It causes drowsiness, but not a wide QRS, fits or big pupils.

lq: Which overdose widens the QRS and is treated with bicarbonate?

q: What operation did she have yesterday?
s: Mrs. Shereen, 41, had a big goiter pressing on her windpipe and had an operation on her neck yesterday. Today she has tingling around her mouth and in her fingers, and cramps in her hands. When the nurse pumps up the blood pressure cuff, her hand goes into a spasm. Her calcium is low.
c: Neck surgery for a goiter, then tingling, cramps and a hand spasm under the cuff, with low calcium.

a.w: The tiny parathyroid glands sit next to the thyroid and can be bruised or removed, so calcium falls after surgery.
It is near the ear and can affect the face nerve, not calcium.
A breathing tube that doesn't touch the parathyroids.
It is in the belly and doesn't drop calcium like this.

lq: Why can calcium fall after thyroid surgery?
la: The parathyroid glands may be bruised or removed

q: What was done during the test?
s: Mr. Khairy, 58, had a home stool test that showed hidden blood. A camera was passed into his large bowel, and the doctor found a small growth on a stalk. A wire loop was tightened around its stalk and it was cut off through the camera. The lab says it was not cancer yet, but could have become one. He has a repeat camera in three years.
c: A growth on a stalk, a wire loop through the camera, and a repeat test in three years.

a.w: Removing polyps through the camera stops them turning into bowel cancer.
Open surgery, not done through the camera for a small polyp.
Bands tie off varices or piles, not polyps.
Not needed for a polyp that is not cancer.

lq: How are bowel polyps removed?

q: What protects her baby's brain?
s: Mrs. Nermin, 28, has phenylketonuria and stopped her special diet as a teenager. Before trying for a baby, her clinic told her to go back on a strict diet and keep her blood phenylalanine low, with weekly tests, before and through the pregnancy. Her baby is born healthy. A friend with the same condition, who didn't, had a baby with a small head and a heart defect.
c: A mother with phenylketonuria, a strict diet with weekly blood tests before and during pregnancy.

a.w: High phenylalanine in the mother harms the baby's brain and heart, even if the baby doesn't have the condition.
It protects the spine, not against phenylalanine.
They prevent anemia only.
It is for diabetes, not phenylketonuria.

lq: What must women with phenylketonuria do before and during pregnancy?
la: Return to a strict low-phenylalanine diet

q: Which blood thinner is safe in her pregnancy?
s: Mrs. Reham, 30, had a clot in her leg last year and has been on warfarin. Now she is six weeks pregnant. Her doctor stops the warfarin at once, because it can harm the baby's face and bones, and starts a daily injection under the skin of her belly. It doesn't cross to the baby, and she doesn't need INR checks.
c: A pregnant woman taken off warfarin and put on a daily injection that doesn't reach the baby.

a.w: It doesn't cross the placenta, so it is the blood thinner used in pregnancy.
Tablet thinners like this are avoided in pregnancy.
Not enough to treat a clot.
It crosses the placenta and can cause birth defects.

lq: Which blood thinner is used in pregnancy?
la: Low molecular weight heparin, such as enoxaparin

q: What protected her baby from the virus?
s: Mrs. Hala, 27, found out she had HIV at her first pregnancy visit. She took daily tablets through the rest of the pregnancy, and her viral load became too low to measure. She had a normal birth, and her baby was given syrup for some weeks. She was advised not to breastfeed. The baby's tests at 18 months are negative.
c: HIV found in pregnancy, daily tablets until the virus was unmeasurable, and syrup for the baby.

a.w: Keeping the mother's virus unmeasurable, with medicine for the baby, cuts the risk of passing HIV to almost nothing.
It was once used, but isn't needed when the virus is unmeasurable.
HIV is a virus; antibiotics don't touch it.
It protects against hepatitis B, not HIV.

lq: What prevents HIV passing from mother to baby?
la: Antiretroviral therapy for the mother, and medicine for the baby

q: What operation was done on his arm?
s: Mr. Sherif, 55, has kidneys that are slowly failing and will need dialysis soon. Two months ago, a surgeon joined a vein to an artery at his wrist. Now the vein on his forearm is big and firm, and a buzzing feeling runs through it under the fingers. The nurses never take blood pressure or blood from that arm.
c: A vein joined to an artery at the wrist, a big buzzing vein, and an arm kept for dialysis.

a.w: Joining an artery to a vein makes a strong vein for dialysis needles. The buzz is the blood rushing through.
It goes in the lower belly, not the arm.
A tube in a neck vein, not an operation joining vessels.
A tube in the belly, not the arm.

lq: What is made in the arm for long-term hemodialysis?

q: What treatment was put in his brain?
s: Mr. Raafat, 60, has had Parkinson's for 12 years. His tablets now wear off fast, and he swings between stiff and wriggling. He had an operation where thin wires were placed deep in his brain and connected to a small battery box under the skin of his chest. With the box switched on, his tremor and wriggling settled and he needs fewer tablets.
c: Long-standing Parkinson's, wires deep in the brain and a battery box under the chest skin.

a.w: Electrical pulses to deep brain areas ease tremor and swings when tablets no longer work well.
It is a box under the chest skin too, but its wires go to the heart.
Used for some epilepsy, with a wire to a neck nerve, not deep in the brain.
It drains fluid from the brain and has no battery.

lq: What is deep brain stimulation used for in Parkinson's?
la: Tremor and motor swings when tablets no longer work well

q: How was her baby delivered?
s: Mrs. Doaa, 32, had painless bright red bleeding at 34 weeks. Her scan shows the placenta lies right over the opening of the womb. The doctors kept her in hospital and gave steroid injections for the baby's lungs. At 37 weeks, she went to theater for a planned birth, and the baby was delivered safely through a cut low in her belly.
c: A placenta lying over the opening of the womb, and a planned birth in theater through a cut in the belly.

a.w: When the placenta covers the opening of the womb, the baby can't be born vaginally without heavy bleeding.
It would make the placenta bleed heavily.
Still vaginal, so unsafe here.
It would start contractions through the same blocked opening.

lq: How is a baby delivered when the placenta covers the cervix?

q: What treatment protected her sight?
s: Mrs. Eman, 29, has had type 1 diabetes for 15 years and is now 20 weeks pregnant. Her eye check shows fragile new blood vessels growing on the retina in both eyes, which have got worse in pregnancy. The doctor treated each eye with many tiny spots of light on the outer retina, over two visits. The new vessels shrank.
t: Laser in diabetic eye disease in pregnancy
c: Diabetes, fragile new vessels on the retina worsening in pregnancy, and many tiny spots of light on the outer retina.

a.w: Laser spots on the outer retina make the eye stop growing fragile new vessels. It is safe in pregnancy.
It replaces a cloudy lens, not retinal vessels.
They don't treat the retina.
They don't stop new vessels growing.

lq: What laser treats new vessels in diabetic eye disease?

q: What was done for her wrist?
s: Mrs. Thoraya, 68, slipped on a wet floor and landed on her outstretched hand. Her wrist looked like a dinner fork. Under a numbing injection, the doctor pulled the bones back into line, and an X-ray showed them well placed. A hard shell was moulded around her forearm and wrist. She was told to keep it on for six weeks and keep her fingers moving.
t: Plaster cast for a wrist fracture
c: A dinner fork wrist pulled back into line, then a hard shell moulded on for six weeks.

a.w: The bones are put back into place and held in a cast while they heal, about six weeks.
The wrong joint.
A keyhole look inside a joint, not used here.
It doesn't hold the broken bones in line.

lq: How is a well-placed wrist fracture usually treated?
la: Closed reduction and a plaster cast for about six weeks

q: What operation cured him?
s: Baby Yassin, 5 weeks old, has vomited after every feed for a week. The vomit shoots across the room and has no green in it. He is always hungry after vomiting and is losing weight. A small hard lump like an olive is felt in his upper belly. After a small cut was made in the thick muscle at the stomach's outlet, he fed well again.
c: A baby with forceful milky vomiting, always hungry, an olive-like lump, and a cut in the stomach outlet muscle.

a.w: Cutting the thickened muscle at the stomach's outlet lets milk pass into the bowel again.
Not the cause of vomiting in a 5-week-old.
It doesn't affect the stomach outlet.
A weight-loss operation in adults.

lq: What is the operation for pyloric stenosis?

q: Which mood tablet needs extra care in her pregnancy?
s: Mrs. Rasha, 31, has bipolar disorder that is stable on a tablet with blood levels checked every three months. She is now pregnant. Her doctor explains this tablet can rarely cause a heart valve defect in the baby, that her levels need checking much more often because pregnancy changes them, and that the dose may need dropping around the birth.
c: A mood tablet checked by blood level, a rare heart valve risk to the baby, and levels changing in pregnancy.

a.w: It carries a small risk of a heart defect in the baby (Ebstein anomaly), and its level changes a lot in pregnancy and after birth.
An antidepressant often used in pregnancy, with no blood level checks.
It doesn't need blood level checks.
Its level drops in pregnancy, but it isn't linked to this heart valve defect.

lq: Which mood drug is linked to Ebstein anomaly in the baby?

q: What was done to ease her breathing?
s: Mrs. Kawther, 70, has heart failure and has become very breathless. Her X-ray shows a large amount of fluid at the bottom of her right chest. With her sitting up and leaning forward, a needle was put between her ribs at the back, and over a litre of straw-colored fluid was drained. She could breathe much more easily straight away.
c: A large fluid collection in the chest, a needle between the ribs at the back, and straw-colored fluid drained.

a.w: Draining fluid from around the lung lets it expand and eases breathlessness. The fluid is also sent to the lab.
For trapped air, not fluid.
A camera into the airways, not used to drain fluid.
It takes tissue, not fluid.

lq: What drains fluid from around the lung?

q: What was done to her knee?
s: Mrs. Sanaa, 66, has arthritis in her right knee that is swollen and painful despite tablets. At the clinic, the doctor cleaned her knee, put in a needle and drew off yellow fluid, then injected a medicine through the same needle. The swelling and pain settled within two days and stayed better for three months.
c: A swollen arthritic knee, fluid drawn off, then a medicine put in through the same needle.

a.w: Injecting a steroid into the joint calms the inflammation for weeks to months.
A big operation, not a needle at the clinic.
A camera into the joint through small cuts.
There is no infection.

lq: What is injected into a swollen arthritic knee for relief?

q: What was done for his bleeding belly?
s: Mr. Alaa, 27, was stabbed in the belly. In the ER his pressure is 70/40 despite blood transfusions, and his belly is swelling. There is no time for a scan. He is taken straight to theater, where the surgeon opens his belly, packs the bleeding liver and ties off a torn vessel. He goes to intensive care with his belly left partly open, to finish the repair later.
c: A stab wound with low pressure despite blood, no time for a scan, and the belly opened, packed and left open.

a.w: Opening the belly at once to stop the bleeding saves life when the pressure won't hold.
Too slow and limited for a patient this unstable.
Without stopping the bleed, blood alone won't save him.
It can stop some bleeds, but he is too unstable to wait.

lq: What does an unstable patient with a stab wound to the belly need?

q: What should be done first after pulling him out?
s: A boy of 10 is pulled from the sea after going under. On the sand he doesn't respond and isn't breathing. A lifeguard is on the way with equipment, and someone has called an ambulance. His skin is cold and blue around the lips. There is no sign he hit his head.
c: A drowned child who isn't breathing: lack of oxygen is the main problem.

a.w: In drowning, the lack of oxygen comes first, so give 5 breaths before starting compressions.

a.o: Press on his belly to get water out
a.w: It wastes time and can make him vomit.
Only for someone breathing normally.
He isn't breathing; CPR can't wait.

lq: What is different about CPR in drowning?
la: Start with 5 rescue breaths, because lack of oxygen comes first

q: Which heart tablet did he stop?
s: Mr. Kamel, 61, has angina and has taken a tablet every morning for years that keeps his pulse slow. He ran out four days ago and didn't refill it. Since yesterday his heart races at 120, his pressure is high, he feels shaky, and his chest pain has come back several times a day. His thyroid tests are normal.
c: A daily tablet that kept his pulse slow, stopped four days ago, then racing heart and returning angina.

a.w: Stopping a beta-blocker suddenly causes a rebound fast heart, high pressure and worse angina. It is lowered slowly.
Stopping it can raise the pressure, but it doesn't keep the pulse slow.
Stopping it doesn't change the pulse.
Stopping it raises clot risk, not the heart rate.

lq: What happens if a beta-blocker is stopped suddenly?
la: Rebound fast heart, high pressure and worse angina

q: Which cream didn't help?
s: Jana, 5, has crusty, golden-yellow sores around her nose and mouth that spread over a few days. Her mother put on a cream from home that is used for athlete's foot, three times a day for a week, with no change. The doctor gives a different cream for five days, and the sores heal. Her brother caught the same rash from her.
c: Golden crusts around the nose and mouth that spread to her brother, and an athlete's foot cream that did nothing.

a.w: The rash is impetigo, a bacterial skin infection. Antifungals don't kill bacteria.
The antibiotic cream that healed it.
It can also treat small patches of impetigo.
Another antibiotic cream that works for impetigo.

lq: What causes impetigo and how is it treated?
la: A bacterial skin infection, treated with an antibiotic or antiseptic cream

q: What cleared his ear?
s: Seif, 16, swims every day. For three days his right ear has been itchy, then painful, and pulling on the ear makes it much worse. The ear canal is red and swollen with some white discharge, but the eardrum looks normal. He has no fever. He used drops in the ear three times a day for a week and kept the ear dry, and it healed.
c: A swimmer with a painful, swollen ear canal, pain on pulling the ear, and a normal eardrum.

a.w: Otitis externa is an infection of the ear canal. Drops treat it directly; keeping the ear dry helps.
Used for middle ear infections, not an infected ear canal.
For fluid behind the eardrum, which he doesn't have.
It doesn't reach the ear canal.

lq: What treats swimmer's ear?
la: Antibiotic (often with steroid) ear drops and keeping the ear dry

q: What did she have too much of?
s: Rania, 19, came back from a party and was found very sleepy on the bathroom floor. She smells strongly of drink and vomited twice. Her sugar is low at 2.8, her temperature is 35.4, and she groans to pain. Her pupils are normal size and react. She took no tablets, according to her friends.
c: A party, a strong smell of drink, low sugar and low temperature, with normal pupils.

a.w: Too much alcohol makes people drowsy and cold, and can drop the sugar. She needs sugar, warmth and her airway protected.
It shrinks the pupils to pinpoints, and hers are normal.
It makes people agitated and hot, not cold and sleepy.
It doesn't cause drowsiness early on.

lq: What should be checked in anyone drowsy from drink?
la: Blood sugar, as alcohol can cause low sugar

q: Which treatment stopped?
s: Omar, 15, has type 1 diabetes and uses a small device clipped to his belt. After a swimming trip, he forgot to reconnect its tube for most of the day. By evening he is vomiting, breathing fast and deep, and his breath smells sweet. His sugar is 26 and his blood ketones are high. He took no other medicines.
c: Type 1 diabetes, a device on the belt left disconnected for hours, then high sugar and ketones.

a.w: A pump gives only fast insulin, so if it stops, ketones build up within hours. Backup injections are needed.
Missing them wouldn't raise his sugar.
He has type 1 diabetes and doesn't take it.
It treats the thyroid, not sugar.

lq: Why does a stopped insulin pump cause ketoacidosis quickly?
la: It only gives fast insulin, so there is no long-acting insulin in reserve

q: What change fixed his constipation?
s: Mr. Yehia, 34, works long hours at a desk and eats mostly white bread, fast food and little fruit. He opens his bowels every four days, with hard stools and straining. His tests are normal and he has no weight loss or blood. Over a month he added vegetables, fruit, oats and lots of water each day, and now goes daily with soft stools.
c: A low-fiber diet, hard stools, normal tests, and a change to fruit, vegetables, oats and water.

a.w: Fiber holds water in the stool, making it softer and bigger so it moves more easily.
It slows the bowel and would make constipation worse.
It lowers stomach acid and doesn't help constipation.
Not needed for simple constipation.

lq: What is the first treatment for simple constipation?
la: More fiber, more water and more movement

q: What daily treatment keeps her growing normally?
s: Baby Salma's heel-prick test on day 5 showed a very high TSH. She is a little sleepy and slow to feed, with a big tongue and a hoarse cry. A scan shows her thyroid gland never formed properly. She starts a tiny crushed tablet every day. At 3 years old, she is growing and talking like other children.
c: A very high TSH on the newborn heel test, a missing thyroid gland, and a tiny daily tablet.

a.w: Replacing the missing thyroid hormone from birth protects the brain and growth.
For PKU, not the thyroid.
It lowers an overactive thyroid, the opposite.
Not needed once thyroid hormone is replaced.

lq: How is congenital hypothyroidism treated?
la: Daily levothyroxine started as early as possible

q: Why didn't her iron tablets work?
s: Mrs. Heba, 38, has low iron from heavy periods. She took her iron tablet every morning for three months, always with a big cup of strong tea and milk at breakfast. Her hemoglobin has barely moved. She has no blood loss from the gut and no celiac disease. Her doctor tells her to change one thing about how she takes it.
c: Iron tablets always taken with strong tea and milk, and no other cause for poor response.

a.o: Taking iron with tea and milk
a.w: Tea and dairy block iron absorption. Iron is taken on an empty stomach, ideally with orange juice.
Vitamin C helps iron absorption, the opposite.
Timing alone doesn't block it.
Folic acid doesn't block iron.

lq: What helps and what blocks iron tablet absorption?
la: Vitamin C helps; tea, coffee and milk block it

q: What did she take that caused this?
s: Mrs. Aya, 30, took a week of antibiotics for a chest infection, which got better. Now she has an itchy vagina with a thick white discharge like cottage cheese, without a bad smell. c: A week of antibiotics, then itching and a thick white discharge, as after a previous course.

It doesn't change the vaginal bacteria.
It doesn't cause thrush.
It doesn't cause thrush.

lq: Why do antibiotics often cause thrush?
la: They kill helpful bacteria, so candida overgrows

q: What simple change stopped his stones coming back?

c: Outdoor work in the heat, dark urine, repeated stones, and aiming for pale urine every day.

a.w: Plenty of fluid dilutes the urine so crystals can't form stones. It is the main way to prevent them.
Too little calcium can actually raise stone risk.
It adds phosphoric acid and doesn't prevent stones.
High doses can raise oxalate stones.

lq: What is the main way to prevent kidney stones?
la: Drink enough fluid for pale urine, over 2.5 L a day

q: What stopped the fit?

c: A fit lasting over five minutes, and a liquid given into the cheek from a small syringe.

a.w: A benzodiazepine given into the cheek stops a prolonged fit outside hospital.
It lowers fever but doesn't stop fits.
A daily preventer, not a rescue medicine.
It treats low sugar, not epilepsy.

lq: What rescue medicine is given for a fit lasting over 5 minutes at home?

q: What cleared the discharge?
s: Mrs. Shimaa, 28, has a thin grey discharge with a fishy smell, worse after sex. She has no itching or soreness. The discharge tests show a raised pH and "clue cells". She took tablets twice a day for a week and was told not to drink any alcohol with them. The smell went away.
c: A thin grey fishy discharge, clue cells, and tablets taken with no alcohol.

a.w: It treats bacterial vaginosis. With alcohol it causes flushing, vomiting and a racing heart.
It treats thrush, which itches and has no fishy smell.
It isn't the treatment for bacterial vaginosis.
It doesn't treat infections.

lq: Which drug treats bacterial vaginosis and must not be taken with alcohol?

q: What cleared her sticky eye?

c: A red eye stuck shut with yellow crust, normal vision, no pain, and drops four times a day.

a.w: Bacterial conjunctivitis gives sticky yellow discharge. It often clears by itself; antibiotic drops speed it up.
They can make an infection worse and aren't used for a sticky eye.
For high eye pressure, not infection.
For itchy, watery allergic eyes, not sticky yellow discharge.

q: What helped his ankle heal?

c: A sprained ankle with no bone tenderness, and rest, ice, a wrap and keeping it raised.

For fractures, not a simple sprain.
Not needed for a simple sprain.
Heat in the first days can make swelling worse.

It protects against TB, not measles.
It doesn't prevent measles.
It protects against flu only.

lq: Which vaccine protects against measles?

q: What treatment helped her panic attacks?
s: Mrs. Basma, 29, had sudden attacks of a racing heart, shaking and fear that she was dying, several times a week. Her heart tests were normal. She didn't want tablets. c: Panic attacks with normal heart tests, no tablets, and weekly sessions learning to test scary thoughts and face avoided places.

It calms attacks short term but is addictive and isn't a long-term treatment.
It eases shaking but doesn't treat the fear.
Panic disorder isn't treated with surgery.

lq: What talking therapy treats panic disorder?

q: What one change helped his lungs the most?
s: Mr. Ramzy, 55, has COPD and used to smoke 30 cigarettes a day. Six months ago he used nicotine patches and a stop-smoking clinic, and he has not smoked since. His cough has eased, he is less breathless walking to the market, and his yearly lung test is falling much more slowly than before.
c: COPD, patches and a clinic, and a lung test now falling much more slowly.

a.w: It is the only thing that slows the fall in lung function in COPD.
It eases breathlessness but doesn't slow the disease.
They treat flare-ups, not the disease itself.
It helps some with very low oxygen, not the rate of decline.

lq: What is the most effective treatment for slowing COPD?

q: What helped his back the most?
s: Mr. Sameh, 38, has had low back pain for three weeks after moving furniture. There is no numbness, no leg weakness, no fever and no trouble with his bladder or bowels. His doctor told him to keep active, keep working, take simple painkillers and walk every day. In four weeks the pain was gone.
c: Simple low back pain with no warning signs, and advice to keep active and walk daily.

a.w: For simple back pain, staying active and walking speed recovery more than rest.
It slows recovery and weakens the muscles.
Not needed without warning signs, and it doesn't treat anything.
Not used for simple back pain.

lq: What is the best advice for simple low back pain?
la: Stay active, keep moving and use simple painkillers

q: What operation cured her?
s: Lina, 18, has had pain for a day that started around her belly button and moved to her lower right side. She has a fever, no appetite and vomited once. Gallbladder pain is in the upper right.
A hernia is a lump, not this pain.
She isn't pregnant.

q: What should be done first?
s: A boy of 12 cuts his forearm on broken glass in the school yard. Blood is flowing steadily from a cut about 4 cm long. There is no glass left in it that can be seen. He is pale but talking. The teacher has the first aid kit and gloves.
c: A steadily bleeding cut with no glass seen in it.

a.o: Firm direct pressure with a clean pad
a.w: Pressing firmly on the wound for at least 10 minutes is the first way to stop bleeding.
Only for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure can't stop.

a.o: Washing it under the tap first
a.w: It wastes time while it bleeds.
Blood loss is the danger; press it.

lq: What is the first step for a bleeding cut?
la: Firm direct pressure on the wound with a clean pad

q: What treatment years ago damaged his heart?
s: Mr. Medhat, 45, had Hodgkin lymphoma at 19 and was cured. Part of his treatment was aimed at his chest every weekday for several weeks. t: Radiotherapy and the heart, years later
c: Treatment aimed at the chest every weekday for weeks in his teens, then early heart artery and valve disease.

A test, not a treatment, and it doesn't harm the heart.
Short courses don't cause valve disease.
They don't harm the heart this way.

lq: What late heart problems can chest radiotherapy cause?
la: Early coronary artery disease and valve disease

q: Which tablet made his skin burn so easily?
s: Mr. Hazem, 23, is taking a daily tablet for acne. On a beach trip he sat in the sun for an hour, like his friends, but he came home with a painful, blistering burn on his face and arms, much worse than theirs. He never burns like this. His friends, who weren't taking anything, only went a little pink.
c: An acne tablet, and a burn after one hour in the sun far worse than his friends'.

a.w: It makes the skin very sensitive to sunlight, so sunscreen and covering up are advised.
A cream that can dry the skin, but not a tablet.
They don't make the skin burn.
It doesn't make the skin sun-sensitive.

lq: Which acne antibiotic makes the skin burn in the sun?

q: Which treatment didn't help her sore throat?
s: Rawan, 22, has had a sore throat, runny nose, hoarse voice and a mild cough for three days. She has no fever, her tonsils are red but without pus, and her neck glands are not swollen. She was given an antibiotic, took it for five days, and felt no different. On the seventh day the illness went away by itself.
t: Antibiotics for a viral sore throat
c: A sore throat with a runny nose, cough and hoarse voice, no fever, no pus, and an antibiotic that changed nothing.

a.w: A sore throat with cold symptoms and no fever is almost always viral, so antibiotics don't help.
It eases the pain and works for viral sore throats.
They soothe the throat.
They help her recover.

lq: Why don't antibiotics help most sore throats?

q: What antidote is given?
s: Mrs. Nabila, 82, takes digoxin for an irregular heartbeat. After her kidney function worsened, she became confused, vomited and saw yellow halos. Now her pulse is 32 and her potassium is 6.4. Her ECG shows a dangerous rhythm, and the level of her heart drug is very high. Atropine hasn't helped. The doctor orders vials of a special antidote.
c: Very high digoxin, a pulse of 32, high potassium and a dangerous rhythm despite atropine.

a.w: They bind digoxin in the blood and reverse its effects within an hour.
Used for high potassium, but traditionally avoided in digoxin toxicity.
It reverses opioids only.
It reverses heparin only.

lq: What is the antidote for severe digoxin toxicity?

q: Which new drug pushed her sugar so high?
s: Mrs. Thanaa, 66, has type 2 diabetes, well controlled on metformin. A week ago she was given a daily tablet for a flare of her lung disease. Since then her sugar has risen to 22 every afternoon, she is thirsty and passing a lot of urine. There are no ketones and no infection in her urine.
c: Well-controlled diabetes, a new daily tablet for a lung flare, then high afternoon sugars.

It raises sugar only a little.
It doesn't raise sugar like this.
It doesn't raise sugar.

lq: How do steroid tablets affect diabetes?
la: They raise blood sugar, often most in the afternoon

q: Which tablet should not have been given for his diarrhea?
s: Mr. Hamdi, 70, was in hospital for a chest infection and got diarrhea after antibiotics. Without testing, he was given a tablet to stop the diarrhea. c: Diarrhea after antibiotics, a stopper tablet given before testing, then a swollen belly and C. difficile.

The right treatment for C. difficile.
Safe and helpful in diarrhea.
It doesn't stop the bowel.

lq: Why is loperamide avoided in C. difficile diarrhea?

q: What treatment years ago affects his fertility?
s: Mr. Kareem, 30, had leukemia at 10 and was cured after two years of strong medicines through drips and tablets. He and his wife have tried for a baby for two years. c: Two years of strong drip medicines for childhood leukemia, then almost no sperm and damaged testes.

They don't harm fertility.
They don't cause lasting infertility.
It doesn't harm sperm.

lq: Why is fertility preservation offered before chemotherapy?

q: Which stomach tablet weakened his clopidogrel?
s: Mr. Sabry, 63, had a stent put in his heart artery and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. His GP added a tablet to protect his stomach. His heart doctor quickly swaps it for a different stomach tablet, saying this one blocks the liver enzyme that switches clopidogrel on. The new one is pantoprazole.

The safer stomach tablet he was switched to.
An antacid that doesn't block the enzyme.
It doesn't block this enzyme much.

lq: Which PPI weakens clopidogrel?

q: Which antibiotic must not be mixed with calcium drips in newborns?
s: Baby Yousef, 10 days old, is in the neonatal unit with suspected sepsis and needs IV calcium for low calcium. The pharmacist stops the planned antibiotic for him and suggests cefotaxime instead. t: Ceftriaxone with calcium in a baby
c: A newborn on IV calcium, and an antibiotic that forms crystals with calcium.

The safer choice suggested.
Often used in newborn sepsis, and it doesn't crystallize with calcium.
Often used in newborns, and it doesn't do this.

lq: Which antibiotic is avoided with IV calcium in newborns?

q: Which transplant drug is slowly harming his new kidney?
s: Mr. Ehab, 52, had a kidney transplant eight years ago. He takes several tablets to stop rejection, one of which has its blood level checked often. c: Transplant drugs, thick gums, more hair, high pressure and a slowly scarring kidney with no rejection.

a.w: It protects against rejection but can slowly scar the kidney, raise pressure, thicken gums and grow hair.

It affects the blood count and gut, not the kidneys like this.
It can also thicken gums, but it doesn't scar the kidney.

lq: Which transplant drug can scar the kidney and thicken the gums?

q: What made his headaches worse?
s: Mr. Hossam, 40, has had headaches for years and takes painkillers almost every day, sometimes with codeine, to keep going. Now he has a headache 25 days a month, worse on waking. A migraine preventer he wasn't taking.
It wouldn't cause headaches.
His eye check is normal.

lq: What causes medication overuse headache?
